items.q: Which plaque features define vulnerability to rupture?
o: Thin cap, large necrotic core and macrophage inflammation
items.exp: Vulnerable plaques combine a thin fibrous cap, large necrotic lipid core and active macrophage inflammation whose enzymes weaken the cap. Heavily calcified thick capped plaques are more stable.
r: Incorrect. That describes a stable plaque.
Correct. Thin cap plus large core plus inflammation means vulnerable.
Incorrect. Calcification alone does not define vulnerability.
Incorrect. Lipid core is central to vulnerable lesions.
items.kp: Vulnerable equals thin cap, big core, hot inflammation.

items.q: Foam cells in atheroma are mainly which cell stuffed with lipid?
items.exp: Monocyte derived macrophages scavenge oxidised LDL without feedback control, becoming foam cells that form fatty streaks and plaque cores. Smooth muscle cells also accumulate lipid later but macrophages dominate.
r: Incorrect. Smooth muscle contributes but is not the main foam cell.
Correct. Macrophages stuffed with oxidised LDL are foam cells.
Incorrect. Endothelium lines the surface and does not form foam cells.
Incorrect. Platelets form thrombus, not foam cells.
items.kp: Foam cell equals lipid laden macrophage.

items.q: Most acute myocardial infarctions follow which plaque event?
o: Slow growth to total chronic occlusion
Rupture or erosion with superimposed thrombosis
items.exp: Acute infarction usually follows abrupt rupture or erosion of a plaque (often previously non severe) with occlusive thrombosis. Chronic total occlusion more often causes stable symptoms with collaterals.
r: Incorrect. Gradual occlusion allows collateral compensation.
Correct. Rupture or erosion plus thrombosis causes infarction.
Incorrect. Calcification without thrombosis rarely infarcts acutely.
Incorrect. Pure spasm is an uncommon minority mechanism.
items.kp: Acute MI means plaque disruption plus clot, not slow narrowing.

items.q: Malignant hypertension vessel change is best described as what?
o: Hyperplastic onion skin arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis
items.exp: Malignant hypertension produces hyperplastic (onion skin) arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis, causing renal failure, retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy. Benign hypertension gives hyaline change instead.
r: Incorrect. Hyaline change marks benign chronic hypertension.
Correct. Onion skin plus fibrinoid necrosis means malignant hypertension.
Incorrect. Medial calcification (Monckeberg) spares the lumen.
Incorrect. Foam cell plaque is atherosclerosis of larger arteries.
items.kp: Malignant pressure: onion skin and fibrinoid necrosis.

items.q: Abdominal aortic aneurysm most characteristically sits where and ruptures how?
o: Above renal arteries; risk unrelated to size
Below renal arteries; rupture risk rises with diameter
In the thoracic aorta after dissection only
At the aortic bifurcation into iliacs only
items.exp: Atherosclerotic abdominal aneurysms are infrarenal, and rupture risk climbs steeply as diameter exceeds about 5.5 cm, guiding surveillance and elective repair thresholds by protocol.
r: Incorrect. Most are infrarenal and size drives risk.
Correct. Infrarenal location with diameter dependent rupture risk.
Incorrect. Thoracic aneurysms have different causes and management.
Incorrect. The sac spans the infrarenal aorta, not only bifurcation.
items.kp: AAA: infrarenal, and bigger means more likely to burst.

items.q: Tearing chest pain radiating to the back with pulse deficits suggests dissection. What is the lesion?
o: Intimal tear with blood splitting the aortic media
items.exp: Aortic dissection begins with an intimal tear letting blood split the media into true and false lumens, compromising branch vessels. It is distinct from aneurysm dilation and coronary events.
r: Incorrect. That describes myocardial infarction pain without pulse deficits.
Correct. Media splitting from an intimal tear is dissection.
Incorrect. Rupture causes collapse and pain but not a propagating false lumen.
Incorrect. Coronary erosion causes infarction, not aortic pulse deficits.
items.kp: Tearing back pain plus pulse loss equals dissection until disproven.

items.q: Berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis rupture causing which emergency?
items.exp: Saccular berry aneurysms at circle of Willis bifurcations rupture into the subarachnoid space causing thunderclap headache. Associations include adult polycystic kidney disease and connective tissue disorders.
r: Incorrect. Epidural bleeding follows middle meningeal artery trauma.
Correct. Berry rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Incorrect. Subdural bleeding follows bridging vein tears.
Incorrect. Ventricular extension may occur but is not primary.
items.kp: Berry aneurysm rupture means subarachnoid blood and thunderclap pain.

items.q: Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis differs from atherosclerosis how?
o: It occludes the lumen with lipid plaque
Medial calcification stiffens arteries without narrowing the lumen
It causes aneurysms of the aorta
It affects veins of elderly diabetics
items.exp: Monckeberg sclerosis calcifies the media of muscular arteries in ageing and diabetes, producing pipestem vessels without luminal narrowing or clinical ischaemia, unlike intimal atherosclerosis.
r: Incorrect. Luminal lipid plaque defines atherosclerosis instead.
Correct. Medial calcium stiffens but does not narrow.
Incorrect. Aneurysm follows medial degeneration, not this calcification.
Incorrect. It is arterial, not venous.
items.kp: Medial calcium without narrowing: Monckeberg, clinically quiet.

items.q: Healed plaque ruptures contribute to stenosis progression by which mechanism?
o: Layered thrombus organisation adds tissue stepwise
items.exp: Silent ruptures heal by organising superimposed thrombus into the plaque, adding layers that progressively narrow the lumen between clinical events. Stenosis therefore grows in steps, not smoothly.
r: Incorrect. Healing adds, not removes, plaque tissue.
Correct. Organised thrombus layers grow plaque stepwise.
Incorrect. Calcification marks chronicity without dissolving lesions.
Incorrect. Collaterals bypass, not shrink, arteries.
items.kp: Plaques grow by silent rupture and healing cycles.

items.q: LDL oxidation matters in atherogenesis because oxidised LDL does what?
o: Is avidly scavenged by macrophages and injures endothelium
items.exp: Oxidised LDL is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors without feedback, creating foam cells, and is cytotoxic and chemotactic, sustaining intimal inflammation. Native LDL uptake is regulated by contrast.
r: Incorrect. Scavenger uptake is uncontrolled and increased.
Correct. Oxidised LDL drives foam cells and inflammation.
Incorrect. It promotes, not prevents, immune recruitment.
Incorrect. Inflammation weakens caps through proteases.
items.kp: Oxidised LDL is the unregulated macrophage meal.
